I don't know if an experienced eye can make out what this little spider is, but the large web was so complex and distinctive, I thought I'd at least try to get a decent photograph of them. The spider herself was only on the order of about 15-20 millimeters across (leg-span) I would estimate, but on a large web, maybe 60 centimeters in diameter, and more than a meter above the ground, hanging in a not quite vertical plane, with several different woven patterns incorporated. The central circular area was on an entirely different scale and patterns than the rest, and there seemed to be a few radial zones that employed variations on the general plan. 

Photographically, this was a challenge I was not well equipped for, so I have only a couple views to offer. 

This was along a shady footpath just above the floodplain of the Enlow Fork of Wheeling Creek, between two occasionally bushhogged fields, surrounded by Appalachian mixed mesophytic deciduous forest, at an elevation around 289 meters (948 feet).

The orchard spider is a colorful, delicate spider that makes circular webs that are usually positioned horizontally or at an angle. The web is often oriented horizontally, with the spider hanging down in the center. It is usually constructed in low bushes or branches, and is frequently found in sunny, but moist, temperate locations. 
The genus name Leucauge is from Greek roots that literally mean “with a bright gleam”. Leucauge species can be differentiated from other tetragnathids by their oval bodies and reddish-orange triangular markings on the ventral aspect (underside) of the abdomen.
